chunks: Laying out power supply components. The question: What are some considerations when laying out power supply components?
A switching power supply works only if its board layout is right. You sort the circuit by what each part does. The input capacitor and the two switches carry fast, pulsed current.
The switch node swings the full input voltage in nanoseconds. The feedback and control pins are sensitive and quiet.
You place and route in that order: the fast current loop first, then the switch node, then the inductor and output, then the sensitive pins.
Think of a busy restaurant kitchen. The fryer and the stove are loud and hot, so they get the best-ventilated spot and are kept close together.
The pastry station, which needs calm and precision, goes at the far end. A solid floor under everything carries all the foot traffic.
A layout that puts the pastry bench beside the fryer will ruin the cake, even if the recipe is perfect.
The boxed loop (input capacitor, high-side and low-side FETs) carries the pulsed current.
The inductor and output capacitor carry smooth current, so their wiring is about resistance, not inductance.
The switch node between the FETs and the inductor swings the full input voltage.
Hot loop: the loop of input capacitor and both switches. It carries pulses of the full load current ("Routing the buck input capacitor").
Switch node (SW): the node joining the switches and the inductor. Its voltage swings very fast (high dV/dt) ("Routing the buck switch node").
Feedback (FB) node: a high-impedance pin that tells the chip the output voltage ("Routing the buck feedback network").
Ground plane: a solid copper layer under the power stage that carries the returns ("Ground plane pros and cons").
Exposed pad: the chip's bottom pad for heat and ground ("Reducing component heating on the board").
Take 5 amps switching in 3 nanoseconds, so di over dt about 1. 7 times 10 to the 9 amps/s.
If the hot loop has 3 nanohenries of inductance, the spike is L di over dt equals 3 nanohenries times 1. 7 times 10 to the 9 equals 5 volts. With 1 nanohenries it is only about 1.
7 volts. So the input capacitor goes right at the chip's VIN and ground pins, with a solid plane below. That is the whole idea.
"I lay it out in priority order. The hot loop first: input capacitor right at VIN and ground pins, with both switches, so the loop is tiny.
Then the switch node, short and compact with no vias or sensitive routing near it, then the inductor and output capacitors.
The feedback divider and compensation go close to their pins on the quiet side, away from the switch node.
A solid ground plane sits underneath, and the exposed pad gets copper and thermal vias. I check against the datasheet layout example."
